transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-04-22
Start: 20:30 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Lina (Redwood SE), Jordan (NimblePath Product Eng), Priya (NimblePath DevOps), Carlos (CTO)

Auto Summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect):
Quick SDK walkthrough for Python and TypeScript, emphasize storing API keys in env/CI secrets, option to use service accounts and KMS for private deploys; demo toggling between hosted api and dedicated endpoint in a CI pipeline.

Topics: SDK install, auth methods, local vs CI secret handling, predefined quickstart repo, Redwood Console demo, Optimize tips for batching & quantization.

Transcript:
[00:00] Samir (Redwood AE): hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'll do a quick context check. nimble path, Jordan I think you were building the chat summarization pipeline, is that right?
[00:06] Jordan (Customer): yeah that's right, we have a service that ingests support transcripts, we want to run summaries and action extraction, ideally in near real-time.
[00:11] Priya (Customer): and main constraints are data residency and CI secret management, we need to ensure keys never leak into logs.
[00:17] Samir: great, Lina is our solutions engineer, she'll lead the SDK bits and demo the pipeline. quick question on timeline — are you hoping to pilot next month?
[00:24] Carlos (Customer): yeah, roughly 4 weeks, assuming security checks are green.
[00:27] Lina (Redwood SE): ok cool, I'll share my screen in a sec. first high level: we support both Python and TypeScript SDKs, and the auth patterns we recommend are either API key in env var for dev, or service account tokens + KMS-wrapped secrets for CI and private deploys.
[00:41] Jordan: could you show the concrete steps for local dev then CI? often docs skip the subtle parts.
[00:46] Lina: sure — starting with Python quickstart. pip install redwood-sdk (note: actual package name is redwood or redwood-inference, small transcript mismatch sometimes)
[00:53] Lina: code snippet (spoken):
  import os
  from redwood import Client
  client = Client(api_key=os.environ.get('REDWOOD_API_KEY'))
  resp = client.generate('summarize: ...')
[01:06] Jordan: so we just set REDWOOD_API_KEY locally?
[01:08] Lina: yes for local dev. we recommend a per-developer scoped key. in CI, you should store the key in your pipeline secrets and mount it as an env var at runtime.
[01:17] Priya: what about rotating keys and KMS? we use AWS KMS for encryption at rest.
[01:21] Lina: good — for that use service accounts. Redwood supports service account tokens which you can encrypt with AWS KMS and decrypt in CI at job start. the pattern is: store the encrypted blob in your secret store, decrypt using KMS key, then set REDWOOD_API_KEY in the job environment. avoids putting plaintext in repo.
[01:35] Samir: to add, for private deployments we can integrate with your KMS/HSM and vault, and we expose audit logs so you can see which token used which calls.
[01:43] Priya: audit logs — are they per-token?
[01:45] Lina: yes, token-level logs in the Console; we also have routing tags so you can map usage back to pipeline id. small note, the transcript sometimes says 'token level cost' as 'token level cause' — ignore that.
[01:55] Jordan: can you show TypeScript example?
[01:57] Lina: absolutely — in node it's:
  import { Redwood } from 'redwood-js'
  const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY })
  const res = await client.generate({ prompt: 'summarize...' })
[02:12] Jordan: nice. is the SDK promise-based? any streaming support?
[02:15] Lina: streaming is supported — the TS SDK exposes an event emitter for token stream, and Python has an iterator you can consume. that matters if you want sub-200ms first-token latency in the UI.
[02:25] Carlos: latency vs cost — we will probably want to batch some of our workloads. can the SDK play nicely with batching?
[02:30] Lina: yes the SDK integrates with Redwood Optimize suggestions — we can recommend batch sizes and quantization per model. also runtime supports automatic batching but you can set a max wait time and token limits.
[02:40] Priya: for the pipeline demo, can you show how to flip between hosted and dedicated endpoints? we need to test both.
[02:46] Lina: demo coming up — the quickstart repo uses an env var REDWOOD_ENV=hosted|dedicated and in the pipeline we swap the endpoint URL based on that. code sample (spoken):
  ENDPOINT = os.environ.get('REDWOOD_ENDPOINT', 'https://api.redwood.com')
  client = Client(api_key=os.environ.get('REDWOOD_API_KEY'), endpoint=ENDPOINT)
[03:05] Samir: small gotcha — dedicated endpoints have a different auth pattern if you use mTLS or VPC peering, we'll put specifics in the repo.
[03:12] Jordan: will latency change a lot when switching?
[03:14] Lina: dedicated generally yields lower and more consistent p99, hosted has better elasticity. for your near-real-time pipeline I'd suggest dedicated if you need strict SLOs, otherwise hosted with caching & Optimize is often cheaper.
[03:26] Priya: about secrets in logs, we use GitHub Actions — any specific advice?
[03:30] Lina: GitHub Actions: set secrets in repo/org settings, reference via env: REDWOOD_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.REDWOOD_API_KEY }}. never echo the env var in logs. if you need to pass keys to ephemeral runners, decrypt in a step and ensure no-runner persists. we also recommend setting Vault or SSM parameters for rotating keys.
[03:45] Carlos: any RBAC we should know about? we have separate infra and ML teams.
[03:49] Samir: in Console you can create API keys with scopes and expiration; combine with SSO and SCIM sync so users get proper roles. we'll share the doc for SAML/SSO and role mapping.
[03:58] Jordan: can we do a quick look at Console UI for keys and audit logs?
[04:00] Lina: switching to Console — (screen share) top-right is account -> API keys, you can create 'dev-key', 'ci-key', or 'pipeline-key'. you can restrict by model and rate.
[04:14] [04:15] (slight cross talk) Priya: are there rate limits per-key?
[04:17] Lina: yes default rate limits apply, but for Dedicated we can set higher limits and shard keys. also can enable fallback policies.
[04:25] Jordan: what's the recommended model for our extraction workload? we need reliable factual extraction not hallucination.
[04:30] Lina: we typically recommend an instruction-tuned model, run evals on your prompt set using Redwood Optimize. there was a small ASR in the notes where 'evals' read as 'elves' — ignore. we'll run a quick eval job against sample transcripts and measure precision/recall.
[04:45] Samir: demo time — I'll walk through a CI job. this is a simplified GitHub Actions snippet we included in the repo:
  name: run-summarizer
  on: [push]
  jobs:
    run-job:
      runs-on: ubuntu-latest
      steps:
        - uses: actions/checkout@v3
        - name: Decrypt service token
          run: |
            echo "Decrypt with KMS..."
            # decrypt step that writes to /tmp/redwood_token
        - name: Run summarizer
          env:
            REDWOOD_API_KEY: ${{ secrets.REDWOOD_API_KEY }} # or decrypted token
          run: python scripts/run_summary.py
[05:20] Priya: so the decrypted token is never committed, we only keep encrypted blob in repo?
[05:23] Lina: exactly. store the encrypted blob (or use your key manager) and decrypt at runtime. in addition, Redwood supports ephemeral short-lived tokens if you want per-run tokens.
[05:32] Jordan: what's the SDK version compatibility? we're on node 18 and python 3.11.
[05:36] Lina: supported versions are node 16+ and python 3.8+. current SDK release notes in the repo mention newer Node runtimes as well.
[05:42] Carlos: security review — will you provide SOC2 docs and contact for attestation?
[05:46] Samir: yes, Lina will share the security pack. we also have SOC2 Type II and can provide SOC artifacts under NDA.
[05:53] Priya: about private deployment — we might look at on-prem later, will the SDK or API change?
[05:58] Lina: the API surface is consistent. for private deployment the endpoint and auth binding differ (e.g., mutual TLS or private control plane tokens). code-level calls remain the same, you just point Client to your private endpoint.
[06:08] Jordan: any gotchas with streaming and serverless functions? we use lambda for enrichment.
[06:12] Lina: streaming to lambdas can be tricky since lambdas have short-lived connections. recommend using a small proxy or step function to handle long streaming connections, or using the sync generate path for small payloads.
[06:24] (short pause)
[06:28] Samir: ok wrapping up — recap of next steps and dependencies.
[06:32] Jordan: thanks that's super helpful.
[06:34] Priya: quick question — pricing for Dedicated, is there a minimum commit?
[06:38] Samir: yes Dedicated is committed capacity, we'll share tiered pricing. for pilots we often use hosted plus a temporary dedicated dev pool if needed.
[06:45] Carlos: let's go ahead and get the security docs and the quickstart repo, then schedule pilot kickoff.
[06:49] Samir: perfect, Lina will drop the links and Samir will coordinate calendar.
[06:52] (end)
